extracted.intended_audience: educated readers and practitioners of natural philosophy / experimental chemistry (17th–18th century audience)
extracted.subtask_description: A chapter-length exposition arguing for the chemical and physical constitution of the air, giving experimental demonstrations and natural-historical examples for how vapours, effluvia, mists, clouds, and winds are produced and behave, with occasional theological reflection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demonstrate inflammable vapours in air by experiment
rubrics_metrics.description: Show that sulphureous or sulphureous-like particles mixed with the air produce inflammable vapours (effluvia) that can be kindled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide experimental instances such as holding a candle over pits or wells (where the air will be immediately kindled), accounts of houses set on fire by such vapours, and reports of persons burnt (e.g., in the Beemster); relate to volcanic exhalations and chymical operations that dissolve sulphureous matter into air.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show fire mingles with air via luminous/phosphorescent materials
rubrics_metrics.description: Use phenomena like lightning and the behaviour of 'phosphorus' (matter distilled from human urine that shines in the dark and will burn with the least warmth) to argue that 'fire mingles itself with air'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe preparation/observation of such phosphoric substances, note that if kept from air they may not shine or burn, and draw the inference that a fire-like principle is present in the effluvia.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establish that volatile alkalis and acids evaporate into and corrode via air-borne particles
rubrics_metrics.description: Argue that volatile and alcaline salts and acid liquors are dissolved into the air and their effluvia are corrosive and detectable by smell.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite examples: soot/harts-horn extracts, glass phials losing content if not well stoppered, acids producing sower smells, acids placed under copper/brass plates producing 'Spanish Green', distilling spirits of saltpetre corroding stoppers and emitting visible effluvia.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demonstrate burning spirits and oils mix with air and are inflammable
rubrics_metrics.description: Show that volatile spirits and oils evaporate and their vapours in air are ignitable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: warming brandy and applying a burning cane/candle ignites its steams; chemists' lutum (seals) that leak reveal effluvia which will catch fire when a candle is held to them; distillation of olive oil (oleum philosophorum) that flames on exposure to air.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide multiple examples that many kinds of particles incorporate into air
rubrics_metrics.description: Assemble natural-historical and geographic examples to demonstrate that numerous and various particles join the air and are transported over long distances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use reports such as the smell of spices at several leagues distance, corrosive air in certain islands that eats iron and stone, and contrasting 'soft' air of other provinces (e.g., Chili) as empirical evidence of diverse airborne particles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show airborne particles can preserve their original properties
rubrics_metrics.description: Demonstrate that substances evaporated or sublimed into the air may, when collected or condensed, reproduce the same properties and composition they had before volatilisation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give experimental evidence from repeated distillations (waters, spirits, quicksilver) and sublimations (sulphur, camphire, benjoin, sal-armoniac, metals) where the condensed products retain prior characteristics; cite Boyle's 'Discourse on the determinate Nature of Effluviums'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Argue that different mixtures of airborne particles yield wholesome or unwholesome air
rubrics_metrics.description: Explain that conjunctions and separations of airborne particles produce differently constituted airs, some wholesome and some harmful or even fatal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide chemical/medical examples: sublimates formed from components (e.g., spirit of common salt and mercury becoming 'sublimate' poison), and conversely the production of medicines (mercurius dulcis) by mixing poisonous effluvia with salt of tartar; reference historical contagion hypotheses (e.g., Nimeguen, Cairo, plague) and Boyle's confirming instances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use controlled experimental apparatus (air-pump) to show mist and fog formation by rarefaction and exhalations
rubrics_metrics.description: Reproduce mists and clouds in a glass globe by altering pressure and adding vapour to show that mists arise from watery vapours and other exhalations when the air is rarified or when vapours are abundant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe the air-pump experiment: include a small vessel with hot water under the globe to supply steams, evacuate the pump so the included air expands and becomes lighter, observe the formation and disappearance of whitish fog on re-admission of air; relate barometer readings (mercury descent) to likelihood of mist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Produce mist/fog experimentally by effervescence (reciprocal action of volatile effluvia)
rubrics_metrics.description: Show that effervescence or the reciprocal action of volatile effluvia in air produces visible mist or smoke.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experiment with two small phials: one filled with spirit of salt-petre (or spirit of common salt) and the other with another spirit (e.g., sal ammoniac); place mouths near each other to mix exhalations and observe a visible mist that is not seen when bottles are separated; compare to fermentation/effervescence phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: Produce fog/mist by precipitation or separation of dissolved substances
rubrics_metrics.description: Demonstrate that precipitation or separation in nearby liquids can thicken and trouble clear air (or produce smell/stinking fogs) by processes analogous to chemical precipitations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: adding salt of tartar to a solution of sublimate or vitriol causes precipitates and loss of clearness; the author relates this to 'stinking fogs' and to chemical preparations such as making 'golden sulphur' from antimony regulus treated with vinegar producing orange/yellow powders and changes in smell and transparency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat clouds as elevated forms of fog
rubrics_metrics.description: Propose that clouds are essentially the same as mist/fog raised to higher regions of the air.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Support with observational evidence: mountain climbers encountering fog that appears as cloud from below, experiments and analogies (gun-smoke appearing as a black cloud), and citations (Varenius, Mariotte) to show clouds can be composed of non-water particles as well as watery vapours.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain the nature and uses of wind as streams of moving air
rubrics_metrics.description: Define wind as a motion or stream of air and argue experimentally and teleologically for its role in dispersing effluvia, ventilating inhabited places, distributing moisture (rains and dews), and enabling human uses (navigation, mills, drainage).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argue by consequence: if air were stagnant the world would be choked by exhalations and vapours; winds transport watery vapours from the sea to land causing rains and supporting rivers; winds power ships, mills, and drainage; employ rhetorical/theological reflection on the providential design of winds.
